headline: GAO Finds Covered Telecom Equipment at Two Agencies
dek: Defense reported three connected instances and blocked external access while six agencies used several methods to search their networks and inventories.

sources.title: Telecommunications: Selected Agencies Have Taken Steps to Address Risks of Equipment Linked to China

lead.creator: Eclypes2008
lead.rightsBasis: The copyright holder released the photograph under the Creative Commons CC0 1.0 public-domain dedication on Wikimedia Commons.
lead.caption: A trailer-mounted mobile telecommunications tower. GAO found that two of six selected federal agencies reported small amounts of covered equipment and were addressing potential risks.
lead.alt: A folded lattice mobile telecommunications tower rests on a dual-axle black trailer outside an industrial building.

charts.caption: Four agencies reported no covered equipment connected to their networks; Defense and Energy reported finding little.
charts.alt: Graphic lists four agencies reporting none and two agencies reporting little covered equipment.

charts.caption: All six agencies used a combination of inventory, network, procurement-record or physical searches since 2019.
charts.alt: Graphic lists six agencies and four search methods used for covered telecommunications equipment.

paragraphs: Two of six selected federal agencies reported finding small amounts of telecommunications or video-surveillance equipment covered by a 2018 procurement ban, according to a Government Accountability Office review.

Defense Department officials identified three connected instances and said the devices had been blocked from external network access while removal work continued. The Energy Department also reported finding little covered equipment and addressing potential risks.
Officials at Homeland Security, Justice, State and Treasury told GAO they did not identify covered equipment connected to their information-technology networks.

The law generally bars executive agencies from procuring equipment made by specified companies, subsidiaries or affiliates linked to the People's Republic of China. It does not prohibit agencies from using covered equipment acquired before the ban.

All six agencies used combinations of hardware-inventory searches, network scans, procurement-record reviews and physical searches between 2019 and December 2025. No single method was used in every circumstance.
GAO cautioned that each method has limits. Network scans may not cover every segment, including classified networks, and procurement records may not reveal components inside a finished device.

Some agency officials cited limited supply-chain visibility and the lack of a comprehensive, authoritative list of subsidiaries and affiliates. Corporate names and ownership can also change over time.

The review covers six agencies selected because they have entities in the Intelligence Community. Its findings should not be generalized to every federal agency or treated as a full inventory of government equipment.

The agency-reported searches identify equipment matching the statutory definition, not evidence that a device was exploited. Counts and risk-remediation status may change after the report's December 2025 evidence window.
facts: GAO reviewed six selected federal agencies.
Four agencies reported no covered equipment connected to their networks.
Defense and Energy reported finding little covered equipment.
Defense identified three connected instances and blocked external access.
All six agencies used a combination of search methods since 2019.
uncertainty: The six selected agencies do not represent the entire federal government.
Search methods have coverage and supply-chain limitations, and the findings do not establish exploitation of any device.
seoTitle: GAO reviews covered telecom equipment at six agencies
seoDescription: GAO found two of six selected agencies had small amounts of covered telecom equipment; Defense identified three connected instances.

headline: 59% of Federal Sentences Were Within Guideline Ranges Through March
dek: Preliminary Sentencing Commission data counted 19,136 within-range cases among 32,390 cases eligible for the comparison.

sources.title: Quarterly Sentencing Updates: Second Quarter of Fiscal Year 2026

lead.creator: Carol M. Highsmith
lead.rightsBasis: The photographer dedicated the image to the public domain; the Library of Congress reports no known restrictions on publication.
lead.attribution: Carol M. Highsmith / Library of Congress
lead.caption: A courtroom inside the Federal Building and U.S. Courthouse in Asheville, North Carolina. Preliminary commission data shows 59.1% of comparable federal sentences were within guideline ranges through March 2026.
lead.alt: Wood benches face the judge's bench in a formal federal courtroom with tall windows and pendant lights.

charts.caption: Among comparable cases, 59.1% were within range, 29.4% below range without a government motion and 4.4% above range.
charts.alt: Graphic lists 59.1 percent within guideline range, 29.4 percent below and 4.4 percent above.

charts.caption: The Commission reported 32,586 cases through March; 196 were excluded from the guideline-range comparison.
charts.alt: Graphic lists 32,586 reported cases and 196 excluded from the guideline comparison.

paragraphs: Federal judges imposed sentences within the applicable guideline range in 19,136 cases during the first half of fiscal 2026, according to preliminary United States Sentencing Commission data.

Those within-range decisions represented 59.1% of 32,390 cases eligible for the comparison. The Commission received 32,586 cases covering Oct. 1, 2025, through March 31, 2026, and excluded 196 from the range table.
Sentences were below the guideline range without a government motion in 9,537 cases, or 29.4%. Another 2,284 cases, 7.1%, were below range after a government motion for substantial assistance.

Judges imposed above-range sentences in 1,433 cases, or 4.4%. The categories describe the sentence relative to the final guideline range and do not by themselves identify the offense, sentence length or reasons in an individual case.
The update covers cases reported to the Commission by the end of the quarter. Late submissions and later corrections can change the totals before the agency publishes final fiscal-year statistics.

Comparisons with older reports require care because Amendment 836 took effect Nov. 1, 2025. The amendment eliminated guideline departures and created an exceptional-degree-of-mitigation adjustment, changing how some outcomes are classified.

The Commission publishes quarterly tables to show the volume and characteristics of federal sentencing before the annual dataset is complete. The report also breaks cases down by offense, district, demographics and statutory penalties.

The percentages are aggregate judicial outcomes, not a measure of guilt, crime prevalence or the quality of any sentence. Federal sentencing depends on statutes, guideline calculations, criminal history and case-specific findings.
Because the six-month data is preliminary and the category definitions changed during the period, it should not be treated as a final trend line for the full fiscal year.
facts: The Commission reported 32,586 cases through March 31, 2026.
Nineteen thousand one hundred thirty-six cases, or 59.1%, were within guideline range.
Nine thousand five hundred thirty-seven cases, or 29.4%, were below range without a government motion.
One thousand four hundred thirty-three cases, or 4.4%, were above range.
One hundred ninety-six cases were excluded from the range comparison.
uncertainty: Quarterly Commission data is preliminary and can change with late reporting or corrections.
Amendment 836 changed the departure framework on Nov. 1, 2025, limiting comparisons with older categories.
seoTitle: 59% of federal sentences were within guidelines
seoDescription: Preliminary USSC data shows 59.1% of comparable federal sentences were within guideline ranges during the first half of fiscal 2026.

headline: NIST Adds 52,000 Chemical Fingerprints to Its Mass-Spectra Library
dek: The 2026 update expands two reference collections used to identify unknown substances in laboratories, manufacturing and forensic work.
entities: National Institute of Standards and Technology

sources.title: NIST Expands Its Library of ‘Chemical Fingerprints’ to Identify Unknown Substances
sources.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology

lead.creator: T. Mak, National Institute of Standards and Technology
lead.rightsBasis: Official NIST image produced by a U.S. government agency and published for public reuse with agency credit.
lead.caption: Vials hold chemicals analyzed for the NIST mass-spectral database. The 2026 update added about 52,000 reference fingerprints across two libraries.
lead.alt: Rows of labeled laboratory vials stand in fitted metal trays on a work surface.

charts.caption: NIST added about 35,000 compounds to the Electron Ionization Library, bringing it above 382,180.
charts.alt: Graphic lists 35,000 additions and more than 382,180 compounds in the electron ionization library.

charts.caption: The Tandem Library gained 17,000 substances and now contains 68,635.
charts.alt: Graphic lists 17,000 additions and 68,635 substances in the tandem library.

paragraphs: The National Institute of Standards and Technology added about 52,000 chemical fingerprints to the two main components of its commercial mass-spectral library in a 2026 update.

Mass spectra are patterns produced when an instrument ionizes a substance, breaks it into charged fragments and sorts those fragments by mass-to-charge ratio. Laboratories can compare an unknown sample against the reference collection.
NIST added roughly 35,000 compounds to the Electron Ionization Library, bringing its total above 382,180. That collection is designed for compounds that can be vaporized for analysis.
The Tandem Library, used for nonvolatile compounds dissolved in liquids, gained 17,000 entries and now contains 68,635 substances.

Researchers and manufacturers use the resource to identify materials in food, drugs, cosmetics, environmental samples, body fluids, forensic evidence and extraterrestrial samples. NIST has maintained the library since 1988.
The new entries include minor cannabinoids, nitazenes, sulfur-bearing thiophenes, complex organic compounds found in asteroid Bennu samples and an expanded set of PFAS reference spectra.

NIST says software-based evaluation and expert review are used to check the library before release. The product, commonly called NIST26, is licensed through instrument manufacturers and independent distributors rather than offered as an unrestricted download.

A larger reference library increases the set of compounds that can potentially be matched, but it does not guarantee identification of every unknown. Sample quality, instrument settings and similarity among spectra still affect results.
The totals refer to library entries, not unique substances encountered in the environment or proof that a listed compound was present in any specific sample.
facts: NIST added about 35,000 compounds to the Electron Ionization Library.
That library now contains more than 382,180 compounds.
The Tandem Library gained 17,000 substances.
The Tandem Library total is 68,635.
NIST has maintained the mass-spectral library since 1988.
uncertainty: A reference match depends on sample quality and instrument conditions and is not guaranteed for every unknown.
Library-entry totals do not measure the prevalence of compounds in real-world samples.
seoDescription: NIST added about 52,000 mass spectra to two chemical reference libraries used to identify unknown substances.

headline: Census Releases New Household Tables From a 136,000-Home Survey
dek: The experimental March 2026 release covers jobs, energy costs, well-being, prices and other fast-moving household conditions.
entities: Household Trends and Outlook Pulse Survey

sources.title: Census Bureau Releases New Data Tables From the Household Trends and Outlook Pulse Survey

lead.creator: United States Census Bureau
lead.rightsBasis: Photograph created by a U.S. Census Bureau employee in the course of official duties and marked public domain on Wikimedia Commons.
lead.caption: The U.S. Census Bureau headquarters in Suitland, Maryland. The bureau released March 2026 household-trends tables based on responses from about 136,000 households.
lead.alt: The glass-and-wood facade of the United States Census Bureau headquarters curves beside a landscaped plaza.

charts.caption: The March survey included about 136,000 households and questions spanning employment, expenses, energy and well-being.
charts.alt: Graphic lists about 136,000 households and survey topics including employment, expenses, energy and well-being.

charts.caption: HTOPS is an experimental product designed to collect and release timely household data every other month.
charts.alt: Graphic labels the household survey an experimental product with an every-other-month cycle.

paragraphs: The Census Bureau released a new set of tables from roughly 136,000 households that responded to its Household Trends and Outlook Pulse Survey in March 2026.
The experimental survey is designed to measure changing social and economic conditions faster than the bureau's longer-running annual products. Data is collected and released every other month.
The March tables cover employment, household energy use and expenses, mental health, social connectedness, arts participation, prices, household expenses and financial stress.
Census published national estimates and tables for smaller geographic areas. The release is intended to give agencies, researchers and communities a more current view of household conditions.
The product continues the bureau's rapid-response survey work while using a redesigned name and schedule. Its questionnaires can change between cycles as information needs change.

A sample of 136,000 responding households is large, but survey estimates still carry sampling error and can be affected by nonresponse, weighting and question wording. Tables should be read with their technical notes and margins of error.
The release does not mean the Census Bureau contacted every household or produced a count of every person experiencing a condition. The tables estimate population patterns from survey responses.

Experimental status means the bureau is still evaluating methods and user needs. Estimates can be revised, and measures may not be directly comparable with statistics from surveys that use different questions or collection periods.
The July announcement covers responses gathered in March, so the results are a snapshot rather than a real-time measure of household conditions in August.
facts: About 136,000 households responded in March 2026.
The tables include national and smaller-area estimates.
Topics include employment, energy expenses, mental health and financial stress.
HTOPS collects and releases data every other month.
The Census Bureau classifies the product as experimental.
uncertainty: Survey estimates are subject to sampling error, nonresponse and weighting assumptions.
March responses do not measure household conditions at the later publication date.
seoTitle: Census releases March household trends tables
seoDescription: Census released experimental March 2026 tables from about 136,000 households on jobs, energy, expenses, well-being and prices.

headline: NOAA Finds Cleaner Urban Air Is Unlocking an Understudied Particle Pathway
dek: Aircraft and satellite measurements suggest falling nitrogen oxides are giving some organic molecules more time to form particle-building compounds.
entities: Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences

sources.title: Understudied Chemistry May Already Be Adding to Urban Particulate Pollution
Fate of isoprene peroxy radical constrains the urban photochemical regime

lead.creator: Elizabeth Holloway
lead.rightsBasis: The photographer released the image under the Creative Commons CC0 1.0 public-domain dedication on Wikimedia Commons.
lead.caption: Downtown Los Angeles seen through haze in 2023. New aircraft and satellite research finds that falling nitrogen oxides are changing particle-forming chemistry across North American cities.
lead.alt: Downtown Los Angeles skyscrapers appear through a thick layer of pale gray pollution haze.

charts.caption: Researchers inferred average organic-peroxy-radical lifetimes near 17 seconds in New York, Chicago and Toronto, versus about 7 seconds in Los Angeles.
charts.alt: Graphic compares 17-second radical lifetimes in three cities with 7 seconds in Los Angeles.

charts.caption: The modeled isomerization share was 12% to 17% for alpha-pinene, 44% for 2-ethoxyethanol and nearly 50% for hexanal.
charts.alt: Graphic lists isomerization shares of 12 to 17 percent, 44 percent and nearly 50 percent for three compounds.

paragraphs: Declining nitrogen-oxide pollution is giving some reactive organic molecules more time to rearrange into compounds that can help form fine particles over North American cities, a new NOAA-led study reports.
Researchers combined aircraft measurements from the 2023 AEROMMA campaign with observations from NASA's TEMPO satellite. The flights sampled air over New York, Chicago, Toronto and Los Angeles.

The team inferred that organic peroxy radicals had average reaction windows near 17 seconds in New York, Chicago and Toronto, compared with about 7 seconds in Los Angeles, where nitrogen-oxide levels remained higher.

At lower nitrogen-oxide concentrations, some radicals can internally rearrange and add oxygen through autoxidation. The resulting highly oxidized molecules have low volatility and can condense into secondary organic aerosol, part of fine-particle pollution.

For alpha-pinene, the researchers estimated that 12% to 17% of radicals used the isomerization pathway across the four cities. The estimated share was 44% for 2-ethoxyethanol and approached 50% for hexanal.

The finding does not mean nitrogen-oxide reductions are harmful overall. Those reductions have helped cut ozone and smog, while the net effect of the newly emphasized particle pathway remains an open research question.

NOAA says many air-quality models do not fully represent these reactions because laboratory rate measurements exist for only a limited set of compounds. Omitting them could understate some summer particle formation.

The measurements and calculations characterize atmospheric chemistry during a 2023 field campaign. They do not directly estimate a citywide health burden or show that every neighborhood experiences the same concentrations.

The study identifies a mechanism that may become more important as nitrogen oxides continue to fall. Further measurements and model development are needed to quantify its contribution to PM2.5 under different urban conditions.
facts: Aircraft measurements covered four major North American cities in 2023.
Inferred radical lifetimes averaged about 17 seconds in New York, Chicago and Toronto.
The comparable Los Angeles average was about 7 seconds.
Alpha-pinene isomerization was estimated at 12% to 17%.
Many air-quality models do not fully include the studied pathways.
uncertainty: The study identifies and constrains a chemical pathway but does not calculate a citywide health burden.
The contribution to PM2.5 depends on compound mix, season, nitrogen oxides and other local conditions.
seoTitle: NOAA tracks changing urban particle chemistry
seoDescription: NOAA aircraft and satellite data suggests falling nitrogen oxides are enabling an understudied particle-forming pathway in cities.

headline: IMF Releases $22.5 Million as Gambia Growth Is Projected to Slow
dek: The board completed two program reviews, extended both arrangements and projected economic growth to ease from 6% in 2025 to 4.7% in 2026.

sources.title: IMF Executive Board Concludes 2026 Article IV Consultation and Completes Reviews Under the ECF and RSF Arrangements with The Gambia

lead.creator: bartvanpoll
lead.rightsBasis: Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 2.0 Generic, granted by the photographer on Wikimedia Commons.
lead.caption: A downtown street in Banjul, The Gambia. The IMF approved an immediate disbursement worth about $22.5 million after completing two program reviews.
lead.alt: Cars and pedestrians move along a broad downtown street in Banjul lined with low commercial buildings and trees.

charts.caption: The IMF made SDR 16.58 million, about $22.51 million, immediately available across two programs.
charts.alt: Graphic lists 16.58 million SDR and approximately 22.51 million U.S. dollars in immediate IMF financing.

charts.caption: The IMF estimated 6% growth in 2025, projected 4.7% in 2026 and about 5% over the medium term.
charts.alt: Graphic compares Gambia growth of 6 percent in 2025, 4.7 percent in 2026 and 5 percent medium term.

paragraphs: The International Monetary Fund approved immediate financing worth about $22.51 million for The Gambia after completing reviews of two economic programs in July.

The package totals SDR 16.58 million. It includes SDR 6.22 million, about $8.44 million, under the Extended Credit Facility and SDR 10.36 million, about $14.06 million, under the Resilience and Sustainability Facility.
Total disbursements under the credit arrangement reached SDR 55.97 million, about $75.98 million. Resilience-facility disbursements reached SDR 25.90 million, about $35.16 million.
The board extended both arrangements by six months and augmented the credit program by SDR 12.44 million, equal to 20% of The Gambia's IMF quota.
The IMF estimated that the economy grew 6% in 2025 and projected growth to moderate to 4.7% in 2026 before returning to about 5% over the medium term.
The Fund said inflation was easing and foreign-exchange reserves remained adequate, while warning that global uncertainty, climate shocks, debt pressures and policy slippage could weaken the outlook.
Program priorities include domestic-revenue collection, public-finance management, state-owned enterprises, central-bank governance and measures intended to strengthen climate resilience.

IMF approval and disbursement do not guarantee the projected growth path. The forecast assumes continued policy implementation and is exposed to external prices, tourism, weather and financing conditions.

Dollar equivalents in the IMF release are approximate because Special Drawing Right exchange rates fluctuate. The announcement describes financing to the government, not a direct payment to households or businesses.
facts: Immediate financing totaled SDR 16.58 million, about $22.51 million.
The credit-facility portion was about $8.44 million.
The resilience-facility portion was about $14.06 million.
The IMF estimated 2025 growth at 6%.
The IMF projected 2026 growth at 4.7%.
uncertainty: Dollar equivalents vary with the Special Drawing Right exchange rate.
Growth projections depend on policy implementation and external economic and climate conditions.
seoTitle: IMF releases $22.5 million for The Gambia
seoDescription: The IMF released about $22.5 million after reviews of Gambia programs and projected growth to slow from 6% in 2025 to 4.7% in 2026.
